deep.reconstruction:
The page holds four separate notes.

(1) Diophantine programme, continued from p.19. On the previous page Hilbert proposes to find infinitely many rational points by tangent constructions:
- on rational cubic curves,
- on x^4+y^4=1 (by square roots),
- on the quintic surface x^5+y^5+z^5=1 (via asymptotic/principal tangents).
He now proposes to solve 'all the Euler and Legendre Diophantine problems' by this principle, 'in particular the famous one on orthogonal substitution coefficients'. That is Euler's problem of finding rational or integral orthogonal matrices (e.g. 4x4 integer arrays whose rows and columns are orthogonal with equal square sums, the 'magic squares of squares'), as reported in Legendre, Théorie des nombres II p.140. He adds the aid of Baltzer's Theorie der Determinanten pp.194-195, presumably the Cayley rational parametrisation of orthogonal matrices, O=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1} with S skew (my identification). No computation is carried out.

(2) Bibliographic note. Functions of x admitting a periodic continued fraction expansion; see 'Abel's remarkable paper', Œuvres vol. 1 p.104. This is evidently Abel 1826, 'Sur l'intégration de la formule différentielle ρdx/√R'. There periodicity of the continued fraction of √R(x) is tied to the polynomial Pell equation P^2 - R Q^2 = const and to the integral being expressible by logarithms (pseudo-elliptic integrals).

(3) Goldbach heuristic, a remark on G. Cantor's table (AFAS congress, Caen 1894, verification of Goldbach's conjecture up to 1000).
- Let L = log x. Take the primes ≤ x; there are about x/L of them (Chebyshev order).
- The number of unordered pairs of them is (1/2)(x/L)(x/L - 1) ≈ x^2/(2L^2). Hilbert writes '=' for this leading-order approximation.
- Every such pair sums to an even number ≤ 2x, and there are x even numbers up to 2x.
- Hence the mean number of representations of an even number ≤ 2x is about x/(2L^2). Hilbert states the more cautious 'at least x/(4L^2)'. The extra factor 1/2 is presumably a safety margin, e.g. for using only Chebyshev-type lower bounds for π(x), or for dividing by all 2x integers.
- Since the mean tends to infinity, there are even numbers with arbitrarily many representations as a sum of two primes. This averaging argument is rigorous given a Chebyshev lower bound π(x) ≥ c x/log x.
- Empirical remark from the table: the numbers with (locally) minimal number of representations are all of the form 2^ν p.

(4) Generalised conformal mapping. Hilbert considers maps of a bounded simply connected n-dimensional region onto another such region whose component functions satisfy a system of n linear PDEs. He suggests this is 'the right generalisation of conformal mapping'; in 2D the system is Cauchy–Riemann. He begins an example for n=4, continued on the next page. Implicit motivation (mine): Liouville's theorem makes genuine conformal maps in n≥3 trivial (Möbius only), so one must replace the Cauchy–Riemann system by another linear first-order system.
errors: (1/2)(x/lx)(x/lx - 1) = x^2/(2(lx)^2) is only an asymptotic equality; the dropped term is -x/(2 lx).
The mean computed from x^2/(2L^2) pairs over x even numbers is x/(2L^2), not x/(4L^2). Since Hilbert says 'mindestens', his weaker bound is not wrong, only non-sharp (or deliberately conservative).

The claim that minimal-representation numbers are 'all of the form 2^ν p' is empirical, read off Cantor's table; it is not proved. It is consistent with the later singular-series heuristic, in which the factor ∏_{p|N, p>2}(p-1)/(p-2) is smallest when N has few odd prime factors. Pure powers of 2 (the case p=1) also belong to the minimal class.

results.what: Program to obtain rational orthogonal matrices (Euler's orthogonal-substitution Diophantine problem) via tangent/chord-type constructions and the determinant parametrisation in Baltzer
results.modern_name: Rational points on the orthogonal group; Cayley transform parametrisation; Euler's 4x4 magic squares of squares
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1770), Cayley (1846); Legendre and Baltzer as expositors

results.what: Reference to Abel's theory of periodic continued fractions of √R(x)

results.what: Observation from Cantor's table that the even numbers with minimal number of Goldbach representations are of the form 2^ν p
results.modern_name: Dependence of r(N) on odd prime divisors of N (singular series factor ∏(p-1)/(p-2)), seen in Goldbach's comet

results.what: Proposal that the right generalisation of conformal mapping to n dimensions is a map whose components satisfy n linear first-order PDEs (generalised Cauchy–Riemann system), with n=4 and n=3 singled out
results.modern_name: Generalised Cauchy–Riemann systems / hypercomplex (quaternionic, Fueter-regular; Moisil–Teodorescu in 3D) function theory; also related to quasiconformal maps / Beltrami systems

deep.surprise_reason: These are mostly programmatic notes and references. Two items have modest interest. First, the private Goldbach observation (c. 1894–95) that 2^ν p numbers have minimal representation counts parallels Stäckel and Haussner and the later Hardy–Littlewood singular series; it is an early, unpublished observation by Hilbert, but similar remarks were circulating (Sylvester 1871). Second, the idea of generalising conformal maps via linear first-order PDE systems in n dimensions, especially n=4, foreshadows hypercomplex function theory of the 1930s, but only as a vague programme.

checkable.asserts: The difference is -x/(2L), lower order; Hilbert's equality holds asymptotically.
The actual mean x/(2L^2) exceeds Hilbert's bound x/(4L^2) by x/(4L^2) > 0.

checkable.sympy: r=lambda N: sum(1 for p in primerange(3,N//2+1) if isprime(N-p)); [r(126), r(128)]
checkable.asserts: Goldbach counts: 126 = 2·3^2·7 has 10 representations, 128 = 2^7 has 3, illustrating minima at 2^ν p.

checkable.sympy: r=lambda N: sum(1 for p in primerange(3,N//2+1) if isprime(N-p)); [N for N in range(8,1001,2) if r(N)<min(r(N-2),r(N+2))]
checkable.asserts: Lists strict local minima of r(N) up to 1000; check whether all are of the form 2^k p or 2^k (Hilbert's empirical claim).

checkable.sympy: a,b,c=symbols('a b c',rational=True); S=Matrix([[0,a,b],[-a,0,c],[-b,-c,0]]); O=(eye(3)-S)*(eye(3)+S).inv(); simplify(O.T*O-eye(3))
checkable.asserts: The Cayley transform of a rational skew matrix gives a rational orthogonal matrix (the zero matrix), i.e. a parametrisation of orthogonal substitution coefficients.

transcription_corrections: 'Nim ferner zu Hülfe' should be read as 'Nimm ferner zu Hülfe'.
In the first fraction the denominator was apparently first written differently and corrected to 'lx'; the formula reads (1/2)(x/lx)(x/lx - 1) = x^2/(2(lx)^2).
'Abels merkwürdige Abhandlung Bd 1. S. 104' refers to Abel's Œuvres (Sylow–Lie ed.), vol. 1, p. 104.
